subject: Multiple data sets and a faceting question

messages.author: 801fed5defcadf92
messages.subject: Multiple data sets and a faceting question
parts:
I am using the ggplot2 package quite heavily for implementing
sensible plot methods for some process data objects I am working
on. I have encountered a few issues, which I can't solve or figure
out. I would highly appreciate any suggestions.

a) The key thing is that the process objects hold point process
data as well as discretely sampled continuous process data, and
I am producing the plot basically by superimposing the points
in a suitable way on top of the plot of the continuous process
in a way similar to the following example:

cData <- data.frame(time = seq(0,1,length.out = 100),
value = rnorm(100),
variable = "Cont. Process")

pointValue <- min(cData$value)-0.5

pData <- data.frame(time = cumsum(rexp(8,10)),
value = pointValue,
variable = "Point Process")

p <- ggplot(cData, aes(x = time, y = value, colour = variable)) +
geom_line() +
scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(-2,-1,0,1,2,pointValue),
labels = c("-2","-1","0","1","2",
"Point Process"))

p + geom_point(data = pData)

I have two questions.

a.1) On the legend both geom's appear for both variables. Is there
any way to get only the geom on the legend that is plotted for the
variable.

a.2) Because the different data sets need to be plotted using
different
geoms due to their nature, one of them is "hidden" together with
possible
aesthetics in the geom_point call. In certain cases I find it useful
to
provide different default aesthetics for the points than the global
definition,
but the end user might find that another choice is more appropriate.
My functions return a ggplot object, and I know how a user can easily
override the global aesthetics, but is there any way a user can
override
the aesthetics specified for a particular geom?

b) Another issue is whether there is a mistake in the labels on the
faceted plot in the following example:

exData <- data.frame(time = rep(1:5,4),
id = factor(rep(c(1,2), each = 10)),
variable = factor(rep(c("a","b","a","b"), each =
5)),
value = rep(c(-2,-1,1,2), each = 5))

ggplot(exData, aes(x = time, y = value)) +
geom_line() +
facet_grid(id+variable~.)

I get labels (1,1), (2,2), (b,a), (b,a) and it should be
(1,a), (1,b), (2,a), (2,b). There is a similar behaviour
using facet_grid(.~id+variable)

Best regards, Niels

> a.1) On the legend both geom's appear for both variables. Is there
> any way to get only the geom on the legend that is plotted for the
> variable.
You can use legend = F to turn off the legend for a specific layer.

> a.2) Because the different data sets need to be plotted using
> different
> geoms due to their nature, one of them is "hidden" together with
> possible
> aesthetics in the geom_point call. In certain cases I find it useful
> to
> provide different default aesthetics for the points than the global
> definition,
> but the end user might find that another choice is more appropriate.
> My functions return a ggplot object, and I know how a user can easily
> override the global aesthetics, but is there any way a user can
> override
> the aesthetics specified for a particular geom?

You can use inherit.aes = F in a given layer to not inherit any
aesthetics from the plot - is that hat you're thinking of?

> b) Another issue is whether there is a mistake in the labels on the

No, I don't think so. If we add a column to one of the data sets

pData$cValue <- cData$value[100*pData$time+1]

then I return

but the user might like to see

p + geom_point(data = pData, aes(y = cValue))

This is easy if you know p, but you only know
q <- p + geom_point(data = pData).
Can you change aesthetics for the point layer only
just knowin q? My intention is to _not_ write complicated
plot functions with many options for the user, but instead
to return one default ggplot2 object, and then one can use
all the different ggplot2 functions to modify the object
if needed.

messages.subject: Re: Multiple data sets and a faceting question
parts:
Hi:

I have a more fundamental question: why do you need the legend at all? You've already indicated the point process in your y-axis labeling: why not just make ylab('Continuous process'), perhaps coloring it in the same color as the line plot?

But to answer your question, this seemed to work for me (amazingly enough). I rbound the two data frames to make variable a two-level factor and then did some scale sorcery. There are some changes to your code to add linetype and shape aesthetics.

cData <- data.frame(time = seq(0,1, length.out = 101),
                   value = rnorm(101),
                   variable = "Cont. Process")

pointValue <- min(cData$value) - 0.5

pData <- data.frame(time = round(cumsum(rexp(8,10)), 2),
                   value = pointValue,
                   variable = "Point Process")

allData <- rbind(cData, pData)
p <- ggplot(allData, aes(x = time, y = value, colour = variable,
                       linetype = variable, shape = variable)) +
     geom_line(data = subset(allData, variable = 'Cont. Process')) +

scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, pointValue),
                         labels =  c("-2", "-1", "0", "1", "2",
                                     "Point Process"))

p + geom_point(data = subset(allData, variable = 'Point Process')) +
    scale_colour_manual('Type', values = c('Cont. Process' = 'red', 'Point Process' = 'blue')) +
    scale_linetype_manual('Type', breaks = levels(allData$variable), values = c('solid', 'blank')) +
    scale_shape_manual('Type', values = c('Cont. Process' = 26, 'Point Process' = 16))

You get a bunch of warnings from scale_shape_manual():
warnings()[1]
$`unimplemented pch value '26'`
grid.Call.graphics("L_points", x$x, x$y, x$pch, x$size)

but we fooled ggplot() into doing what you wanted :)

I had hoped that NULL might work, but no. Fortunately, there was a blank linetype. If my little prank with shape = 26 hadn't worked, I was going to try some silliness with alpha transparency, but fortunately that wasn't necessary :)

HTH,
Dennis

Thanks Dennis, I can see how you can do it by "cheating", but
this is hardly a safe solution that I want to put in a package.
But thanks anyway.

On 14/12/10 07.07, Dennis Murphy wrote:
> Hi:
>
> I have a more fundamental question: why do you need the legend at all? You've
> already indicated the point process in your y-axis labeling: why not just make
> ylab('Continuous process'), perhaps coloring it in the same color as the line plot?

This is a relevant question, and there are two reasons. First, I believe that
the difference in color helps the visualization even though the difference is
also marked on the y-axis. Furthermore, other y aesthetics for the points
may be chose, where the difference in color is even more important. Second,
for the general situation I try to handle there are different types of points
that need to be visually separated.

Anyway, I found a thread from Feb. 12, 2010

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2253179/using-ggplot2-how-can-i-represent-a-dot-and-a-line-in-the-legend

were the same question is asked at the end. Hadley replies that at that time it
was not natively supported by ggplot2.

- Niels
